provenance_or_findsite: Tianlongshan, Taiyuan, Shanxi province, China (east sector, far east end of site, >30m from Cave 2)
description: One of the larger caves, believed to be Northern Qi. The facade still has part of the eave over the entrance porch with stone-carved architectural elements (posts, brackets, tiled roof). Interior is a square chamber with niches on the back and side walls, each formerly containing a seated Buddha and two bodhisattvas.

current_location: in situ (Tianlongshan); many wall reliefs removed
description: One of the pair of Eastern Wei caves (Caves 2 and 3). Distinctive for the many relief carvings on walls and ceiling, most of which have been removed.

current_location: in situ (Tianlongshan); wall reliefs largely removed
description: One of the pair of Eastern Wei caves. Distinctive for the relief carvings on walls and ceiling, most of which have been removed.

The largest of the caves at Tianlongshan except for Cave 9; the only central-pillar cave at the site and the only cave known to be of the Sui dynasty. A stele in front of Cave 8 records its creation in the Sui dynasty and is dated 584.

provenance_or_findsite: Tianlongshan, Taiyuan, Shanxi province, China (just west of Cave 9)
description: A Northern Qi cave just west of the colossal sculptures and wooden structure of Cave 9. Like the other Northern Qi caves at Tianlongshan, this is one of the larger caves — interior a square chamber more than three meters on each side with figures carved on all four walls.

The most important Northern Qi cave at the Tianlongshan site. A stele at the entrance to Cave 16, probably Northern Qi, has a mostly-lost inscription. Interior a square chamber > 3m per side with figures carved on all four walls.

One of the most important Tang dynasty caves; remaining sculptures are better preserved than in many other caves. Though damaged and a few completely removed, the carving quality and the original arrangements/poses of the figures remain readable.

current_location: in situ + fragments at Harvard Art Museums (Seated Buddha from Cave 21; Grenville L. Winthrop bequest, 1943), Tokyo National Museum (Seated Buddha with legs pendent, probably Cave 21), Met Museum (Head of a Bodhisattva, attendant from back wall of Cave 21 → object 39640)
description: Among the most heavily-dispersed Tianlongshan caves. The University of Chicago project records >100 sculpture fragments from Tianlongshan across 20+ collections worldwide; Cave 21 is one of the most heavily represented in overseas museum holdings.

title_en: Tianlongshan Caves Project (Center for the Art of East Asia, University of Chicago)
provenance_or_findsite: Tianlongshan (Heavenly Dragon Mountain), 36km southwest of Taiyuan, Shanxi province, China
current_location: project material hosted by University of Chicago
description: 25 caves total at the site (numbered 1–21 for the most important), running ~500m across two sections of a south-facing cliff (Caves 1–8 east, 9–21 west). Project initiated 2013 by the Center for the Art of East Asia at U Chicago to scan and digitally reconstruct dispersed Tianlongshan fragments. As of May 2016 ~100 fragments scanned across 20+ museums worldwide using Artec Group structured-light scanners; digital models reconstruct broken sculptures by joining separated bodies and heads.
